newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Aeroflot seeks to reconquer 'domestic' market.
newsitem.headline: Aeroflot seeks to reconquer 'domestic' market.

text.p: Aeroflot -- Russian International Airlines -- said on Monday it was seeking to reestablish routes within Russia and neighbouring republics lost when the former Soviet monopoly was broken up in 1992.

Leonid Mokhov, Aeroflot's deputy head of marketing, told Reuters that the airline planned to double the number of passengers carried on domestic and regional routes to 260,000 this year from 130,000 carried in 1996.
"This market is very promising and we will develop it," Mokhov said, adding that Aeroflot also planned to start direct international flights from big Russian cities apart from Moscow.
"We are also going to make regular flights from Bryansk in Central Russia to Istambul and from the northern city of Murmansk to Amsterdam," he said.
Aeroflot currently flies to 13 destinations in Russia, former Soviet republics grouped in the Commonwealth of Independent States and the Baltic states.
After the 1992 breakup, which spawned hundreds of so-called "babyflots", the private Vnukovo Airlines became the biggest domestic carrier, while Aeroflot concentrated on international routes.

Mokhov said Aeroflot would begin a regular passenger service from Moscow to Petropalovsk-Kamchatsky in the Russian Far East and from Moscow to Kaliningrad, the Russian enclave on the Baltic Sea, later this month.
Over the past two weeks, Aeroflot has launched scheduled flights from Moscow to Arkhangelsk and Murmansk in the Russian Arctic and to Vladivostok, the Far Eastern port.

Other carriers -- the private Transaero and state-owned Domodedovo Airlines -- currently account for most traffic on the Vladivostok route following the suspension of flights by the troubled Orient-Avia company on July 10.

Mokhov also said that Aeroflot would start flying four times a week between Moscow and Tallinn, the capital of Estonia, from August 15, operating Tupolev Tu-134 jets belonging to private Estonian carrier ELK.
